title: HE DID EVERYTHING “RIGHT”—AND STILL WALKED AWAY FROM JESUS
paragraphs: HE DID EVERYTHING “RIGHT”—AND STILL WALKED AWAY FROM JESUS
Understanding the Rich Young Ruler — Why Being a “Good Person” Wasn’t Enough, and Why His Most Dangerous Possession Wasn’t the Money in His Hands but the Throne in His Heart
Imagine meeting the kind of man most parents would have wanted their daughter to marry.
Young.
Successful.
Respected.
Religious.
Morally disciplined.
Financially secure.
And apparently serious about God.
He wasn't stumbling toward Jesus drunk.
He wasn't being dragged out of some scandal.
He wasn't publicly exposed as an adulterer, thief, murderer, or fraud.
He came looking for eternal life.
And according to Mark's account, he came running.
Then he knelt.
Think about that.
A man with status lowered himself publicly before a wandering Galilean teacher and asked the question underneath every human life:
“Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
It sounds like the beginning of a beautiful conversion story.
But it becomes one of the most haunting encounters in the Gospels.
Because this man came running to Jesus...
and eventually walked away from Him.
Not because Jesus rejected him.
Not because his past was too dirty.
Not because grace was unavailable.
He walked away because Jesus touched the one thing he did not want Jesus to touch.
And before you decide this story is about somebody with a larger bank account than yours, stay with it.
Because the rich young ruler may be much closer to your mirror than you think.

Matthew 19, Mark 10, and Luke 18 preserve this encounter from complementary perspectives. Matthew identifies the man as young. Luke calls him a ruler. All three accounts tell us he possessed great wealth.
But Mark gives us a detail that makes the entire scene almost unbearable.
After the man speaks about his obedience, Mark 10:21 says:
“Jesus, looking at him, loved him.”
The Greek is devastatingly beautiful:
ἐμβλέψας αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἠγάπησεν αὐτόν
emblepsas autō ho Iēsous ēgapēsen auton.
Jesus looked intently at him...
and loved him.
Do not miss that.
What Jesus says next is not cruelty.
It comes from love.
The command that wounds him comes from the Christ who loves him.
Jesus is not trying to humiliate the man.
He is trying to liberate him.
And sometimes the love of Jesus feels like surgery before it feels like healing.
The man had called Him “Good Teacher.”
Jesus immediately pressed the word “good.”
“Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.”
Jesus was not confessing sinfulness. The question forces the man to think more deeply about goodness—and about the identity of the One standing before him.
You are asking about eternal life.
You are calling Me good.
Do you understand what goodness actually is?
Do you understand whom you are speaking to?
The ruler's question contains the assumption that has haunted religious humanity for centuries:
What must I do?
There it is.
Give me the requirement.
Show me the standard.
Tell me the achievement.
Let me accomplish whatever remains.
Because that is how successful people often understand life.
Do enough.
Work enough.
Achieve enough.
Behave enough.
And eventually you earn the thing you want.
But eternal life is not another trophy for the shelf.
It cannot be purchased by morality.
It cannot be negotiated through religious achievement.
It cannot be earned by accumulating enough “good person” points.
Jesus points him toward the commandments.
Do not murder.
Do not commit adultery.
Do not steal.
Do not bear false witness.
Honor your father and mother.
Matthew also records Jesus saying, “Love your neighbor as yourself.”
And the young man essentially answers:
I have done that.
In Mark's wording:
“Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.”
Maybe you recognize something of yourself here.
“I don't cheat on my spouse.”
“I don't steal.”
“I try to help people.”
“I provide for my family.”
“I go to church.”
“I pray.”
“I believe in God.”
“I've never done anything that terrible.”
“I am basically a good person.”
And perhaps compared with another human being, you are.
That is precisely the problem with human comparison.
We keep finding someone worse than ourselves and using that person as evidence that we must be okay.
But your neighbor is not the standard of God's holiness.
Neither is the criminal on television.
Neither is the hypocrite at church.
Neither is your abusive ex.
Neither is the corrupt politician.
Neither is the person whose secret became public while yours remained hidden.
Scripture says, “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
The scandal of the Gospel begins here:
You do not merely need improvement.
You need rescue.
You do not merely need better habits.
You need reconciliation with God.
You do not simply need inspiration.
You need a Savior.
And the Savior was standing directly in front of this man.
Then Jesus placed His finger on the hidden throne.
“One thing you lack.”
Luke records the same terrifying diagnosis.
In Greek:
Ἔτι ἕν σοι λείπει
Eti hen soi leipei.
“One thing is still lacking for you.”
One thing.
Imagine hearing Jesus say that about your life.
Not your pastor.
Not your spouse.
Not the person criticizing you online.
Jesus.
You have built the reputation.
Protected the image.
Practiced morality.
Maintained respectability.
Maybe even learned Christian vocabulary.
But Christ sees underneath all of it.
And He knows exactly what you cannot imagine surrendering.
Jesus tells the ruler to sell what he possesses, give to the poor, have treasure in heaven, and then:
δεῦρο ἀκολούθει μοι
deuro akolouthei moi.
“Come, follow Me.”
That is the center of the encounter.
Not merely:
Sell.
Not merely:
Give.
But:
Follow Me.

Jesus was not presenting poverty as a universal purchase price for salvation, as though heaven could be bought by emptying a bank account. Scripture does not teach salvation by charitable liquidation. Zacchaeus, only a chapter later in Luke, responds to Jesus with radical generosity, but the details are not identical. The early church includes believers who still had homes in which Christians gathered. The Gospel consistently destroys the idea that eternal life can be earned through another human achievement.
The issue is deeper.
Jesus exposed the ruler's god.
The man believed he possessed great wealth.
The encounter revealed that, in another sense, his wealth possessed him.
He could imagine obeying commandments.
He could imagine respecting Jesus.
He could imagine discussing eternal life.
He could even kneel before Christ.
But when Jesus demanded the throne...
the man discovered where his worship really lived.
That is why this story cannot safely remain a story about rich people.
Your idol may not have a dollar sign attached to it.
What is the thing you would obey instead of Jesus?
Your relationship?
Your career?
Your reputation?
Your sexuality?
Your comfort?
Your ambition?
Your political identity?
Your secret habit?
Your bitterness?
Your children?
Your ministry?
Your dream?
Your need for approval?
Your carefully constructed image of being the Christian who has everything together?
What makes you quietly say:
“Jesus, You can have everything except that”?
That “except” may be revealing the throne.
An idol is not merely a statue sitting in a pagan temple.
An idol can be something good that has become ultimate.
Something you love more than obedience.
Something you trust more than Christ.
Something you fear losing more than you fear walking away from Jesus.
Something you cannot surrender even when the Savior says:
“Follow Me.”
And here is the sentence in the story that should break us.
The man became sorrowful and went away.
Matthew says he went away grieving.
Mark describes him as shocked or dismayed by the word and grieving.
Luke says he became deeply sad.
Why?
Because he had great possessions.
He wanted eternal life.
But he wanted something else too.
And when forced to choose, he walked away from Jesus holding the thing that could never save him.
Imagine the silence.
The footsteps getting farther away.
Jesus standing there.
The disciples watching.
The man's wealth still intact.
His reputation still intact.
His morality still intact.
His social position still intact.
And yet he is walking in the wrong direction.
There are losses that look like victories.
You can keep the relationship and lose obedience.
Keep the applause and lose intimacy with God.
Keep the secret sin and lose your tenderness toward Christ.
Keep the money and lose the treasure.
Keep the image and lose the truth.
Keep everything you were afraid to surrender...
and discover that what you protected was never capable of saving you.
This is why “I'm a good person” is such a dangerous place to hide.
Because good compared with whom?
Jesus had already redirected the man's attention toward God as the true measure of goodness.
Scripture's diagnosis is much deeper than “some people behave badly.”
“There is none righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10).
Isaiah describes even our righteous deeds, considered as grounds for standing before the Holy One, as polluted garments (Isaiah 64:6).
The Gospel does not divide humanity into good people who deserve heaven and terrible people who need Jesus.
The Gospel announces something far more humbling—and far more hopeful:
Sinners need Jesus.
Religious sinners need Jesus.
Irreligious sinners need Jesus.
Poor sinners need Jesus.
Rich sinners need Jesus.
Respectable sinners need Jesus.
Scandalous sinners need Jesus.
The addict needs Jesus.
The church member needs Jesus.
The prisoner needs Jesus.
The preacher needs Jesus.
The person whose sin became tomorrow's gossip needs Jesus.
And the person whose sin has remained hidden behind a polished smile needs Jesus.
That is why the disciples' reaction matters so much.
After Jesus speaks of the terrible spiritual danger surrounding wealth and uses the shocking image of a camel passing through the eye of a needle, they ask:
“Then who can be saved?”
Do not soften the image.
Jesus is describing impossibility.
And His answer is the doorway into the Gospel:
παρὰ ἀνθρώποις τοῦτο ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν, παρὰ δὲ θεῷ πάντα δυνατά
para anthrōpois touto adynaton estin, para de theō panta dynata.
“With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
There.
That is hope.
The story is not ultimately teaching you to save yourself by trying harder than the rich young ruler.
The disciples understood enough to ask the right question:
Who, then, can be saved?
Jesus' answer is not:
“The people who work hard enough.”
It is:
What is impossible with man is possible with God.
Salvation is God's work.
Grace is not God's reward for impressive people.
Grace is God's mercy toward people who cannot rescue themselves.
And this is where the road leads to the cross.
The rich young ruler could not let go of his treasure to follow Jesus.
But Jesus would soon continue toward Jerusalem.
Toward betrayal.
Toward mockery.
Toward scourging.
Toward nails.
Toward a cross.
The One who told the ruler to surrender everything was Himself moving toward the place where He would give Himself for sinners.
Paul later writes of Christ:
Jesus did not die because we were already good enough.
He died because we weren't.
He did not rise from the grave to make morally respectable people slightly nicer.
He rose as the victorious Lord who saves sinners, defeats death, reconciles us to God, and calls us into a new life under His lordship.
Christianity is not:
“Look how good I became.”
Christianity is:
“Look how merciful Christ has been to me.”
That changes the way you read this entire story.
Perhaps you have been the rich young ruler.
Not financially.
Spiritually.
You have been close enough to Jesus to ask questions but unwilling to let Him rule.
You have known Bible verses while protecting secret compromises.
You have sung worship songs while negotiating obedience.
You have called Him Lord while reserving veto power over certain rooms in your heart.
You have mistaken conviction for condemnation and therefore run from the very Christ who was exposing your chains because He loved you.
Remember Mark's sentence:
Jesus looked at him...
and loved him.
Christ's exposure of an idol is not evidence that He delights in destroying you.
Sometimes He puts His finger on what hurts because He knows what is killing you.
The surgeon's knife and the murderer's knife may both cut skin, but only one cuts in order to heal.
Maybe Jesus has been touching something in you for months.
Forgive them.
“No.”
Confess it.
“No.”
End the affair.
“No.”
Tell the truth.
“No.”
Stop returning to that pornography.
“No.”
Release your bitterness.
“No.”
Stop worshiping money.
“No.”
Stop building your identity around people's approval.
“No.”
Make restitution.
“No.”
Come out of hiding.
“No.”
Follow Me.
And suddenly the rich young ruler does not feel ancient anymore.
He feels painfully familiar.
This is where repentance enters.
Biblical repentance is not emotional self-hatred.
It is not purchasing forgiveness through tears.
It is not cleaning yourself up sufficiently so Jesus will finally accept your application.
Repentance turns from sin toward God.
Faith rests in Christ.
You stop defending the throne you were never meant to occupy.
You stop presenting your moral résumé as though God owes you eternal life.
You come empty-handed to the crucified and risen Savior.
And you trust Him.
The scandal becomes grace.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The proud can be humbled.
The greedy can become generous.
The sexually broken can become pure.
The liar can become truthful.
The bitter can forgive.
The hypocrite can finally stop pretending.
The ashamed can come into the light.
Not because sin suddenly becomes unimportant.
Precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that Christ went to the cross.
And grace is so astonishing that Christ went willingly for sinners.
This is why Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not merely edit the embarrassing paragraphs of your story.
He gives you a new identity in Him.
The Gospel does not say your scandal was imaginary.
It says your scandal does not have to have the final word.
The cross tells the truth about your sin while simultaneously announcing the staggering depth of God's mercy.
And perhaps the saddest thing about the rich young ruler is that the Gospel account leaves us watching him walk away.
We are not told in these passages that he returned.
So don't invent an ending Scripture does not give us.
Instead, allow the unresolved ending to confront your ending.
What will you do when Jesus touches your “one thing”?
Will you walk away sorrowful?
Or will you finally open your hands?
Because one day every possession you protected will belong to someone else.
Every title will disappear.
Every follower count will become irrelevant.
Every trophy will gather dust.
Someone else will sleep in your room.
Someone else may drive your car.
Your name will eventually disappear from conversations you once dominated.
And you will stand before God with none of the earthly things you spent your life using to prove your worth.
Then the question will not be whether people thought you were a good person.
The question is whether you belong to Christ.
Do you understand why this matters?
You can admire Jesus and still walk away from Jesus.
You can kneel before Him and still refuse Him.
You can be moral and still need mercy.
You can be religious and still need regeneration.
You can know commandments and still resist the King.
You can possess everything the world envies...
and lack the one Treasure your soul was created for.
Jesus Christ.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already broken an idol that once controlled your life, tell someone what His grace did. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to make another struggling person realize they are not alone.
Not because every sentence deserves remembering, but because the question does:
What is the one thing I would rather keep than follow Jesus?
Come back to that question when success starts seducing you again.
Not to win an argument.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
If sharing biblical truth helps another person see Christ more clearly, glorify God with that opportunity.
The Gospel cannot be bought, and supporting a ministry does not save anyone.
Christ saves.
Invite your family. Invite the friend who is struggling. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the person who is searching. Even invite the unbeliever who has questions about Jesus.
But before you leave this article, return one last time to that road.
See the young man.
His hands are still full.
His heart is breaking.
Jesus is behind him.
His possessions are still his.
And he is walking away with everything...
except the One he actually needed.
Don't let that be your story.
Whatever Christ is exposing, bring it into the light.
Whatever sin you have been defending, repent.
Whatever idol you have been protecting, surrender it.
Whatever shame tells you that you have gone too far, look again at the cross.
The Savior who exposes sin is also the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The hands asking you to surrender are nail-scarred hands.
And the Jesus who says, “Follow Me,” is infinitely more valuable than everything you are terrified of leaving behind.
The tragedy was never that the young ruler had too little—it was that he walked away from Jesus believing what he held was worth more than the One who loved him.
